verdicts.reason: Planning fallacy, correctly stated including the direction of the error (people overestimate what they will finish). Hedged with 'reliably poor' rather than a made-up percentage. Age-appropriate and useful.

Small-dose habit framing is consistent with the app's values and safe; the second clause (repetition ingrains whatever pattern is repeated) is ordinary motor-learning and is stated without a fake number. Teaches something real about form.

Firmness defect. 'is what keeps MOST streaks alive' is an unearned proportion — nobody measured what keeps most streaks alive. The underlying idea (implementation intentions / if-then plans help adherence) is supported, but it is stated as a measured majority. Soften to something like 'Deciding in advance what you'll do on the day you don't feel like it is one of the things that keeps a streak alive.'

Two unearned comparatives in one item: 'Kids move most when nobody calls it exercise' (superlative) and 'tends to go on considerably longer' (a quantified duration comparison nobody measured here). The core observation — framing activity as play rather than exercise raises engagement — is plausible but is stated far more firmly than any cited evidence. Also `simplified` with no source for what is really a behavioural research claim.
Hedged ('most children', 'given time, space, and no instructions'), safe, and true of free play at the level of detail given. The closing line is editorial colour rather than a factual overreach.
Properly hedged with 'often'. Side-by-side walking reducing the pressure of a hard conversation is a modest, non-medical claim and is not stated as a measured effect. Safe for all ages.
Household behaviour concordance is real and the item hedges twice ('usually', 'a little'). No mechanism is invented and no proportion is claimed.
Sibling modelling is well documented, and the claim is hedged with 'tend to'. The 'coaches' line is framing, not an invented effect. Safe and age-appropriate.

Stated as a guaranteed outcome: a weekly repeat 'turns it into a landmark that kids still remember years later.' Family-ritual research supports that rituals are valued and remembered, but not that repeating anything weekly reliably produces a decades-long memory. Needs a hedge ('can become', 'often') rather than a promise.
'far more likely' is an unearned magnitude. Choice/autonomy does support intrinsic motivation, but the size of the effect here is invented. Drop 'far' or cite the autonomy-support evidence.
Straightforwardly true (incidental daily activity is real movement), no number claimed, safe, and it usefully reframes existing activity without any body or weight framing.

Safety. The item invites a nine-year-old to race 'to the end of the street' and does not name the traffic hazard, which the rubric requires for anything a child could copy and be hurt by. Relocate it to a safe setting (park, yard, path) or name the condition explicitly.
Warm, safe, non-comparative, and makes a genuine point about modelling across generations. No factual claim to overreach on.
True at the level given and directly aligned with the app's no-comparison stance. States a direction, not a measured effect size.
True, safe, and it reframes chores as movement without any weight or body-composition framing. Modest but it does teach the reframe.

Hedged with 'usually' and framed against adult expectation rather than as a measurement. Children being more fatigue-resistant in intermittent play is well supported, and the boredom half is plainly observational.
Inclusive, safe, no comparison of bodies, and it makes a real point about pacing a group. Nothing to verify and nothing overstated.

'one of the few things' is an unearned superlative and is easy to falsify — a nine-year-old and a sixty-year-old can genuinely cook, play games, garden or make music side by side too. The point survives without the ranking: say movement is one of the things they can do side by side at their own speeds.
Hedged with 'often', and the accountability/telling-someone effect is a reasonable, non-medical claim. No proportion or magnitude invented.

Three firmness problems stacked: 'the MOST reliable exercise partners', 'in MOST households', and the causal 'mainly because'. None of that is measured, and the dog-walking literature is actually mixed — a large share of dog owners do not walk their dog regularly. Rewrite as an observation about the daily prompt a dog provides, without the superlative or the household proportion.
True and non-quantified: playground play does develop balance, coordination and confidence. Safe, and the closing point (it doesn't feel like training) is the actual insight.
Correctly labelled `editorial`, which licenses the firmness of 'is the one that sticks'. Safe, no medical claim, and it says something worth reading to an adult user.
Hedged with 'tend to' on both halves and framed as a comparison against adults' own expectations rather than a measured quantity. Consistent with modelling research.

Verified anatomy: the fingers contain no muscle bellies; flexion and extension come from extrinsic forearm muscles acting through long tendons. The puppet-string image is an accurate simplification, not an invented mechanism.
Verified: 26 bones per foot, 52 of roughly 206 bones, which is genuinely about a quarter. The proportion is one of the few in this packet that is actually arithmetic rather than assertion.
Verified: the malleus, incus and stapes are the smallest bones in the body, the largest about 8 mm. 'All three on a fingernail' is a fair size image, not an invented measurement.

Verified: the femur is the longest and strongest bone, and its anterior bow (a real, named feature) is correctly described as a slight curve rather than straight. Good detail that most readers won't know.

Verified on both halves: the function of yawning genuinely is unresolved (and the item says so, which is the honest handling of an open question), and reading or thinking about yawning is a documented contagion trigger. 'Often' is the right hedge.
'More than six hundred' matches the standard skeletal-muscle count and is loose in the safe direction. 'Dozens at once' for a sit-to-stand is qualitative, not a fabricated number.
Microsaccades and fixational drift are established and the item claims nothing beyond their existence and imperceptibility. Genuinely surprising to a reader, which is what this category is for.

Verified: two lobes on the left, three on the right, and the left lung's cardiac notch really is the heart occupying that space. The 'gave up a lobe's worth of space' phrasing is a simplification of standard anatomy, not an invented mechanism.

'About a minute' is the mainstream resting figure (roughly 5 L blood over roughly 5 L/min cardiac output); published estimates run 20-60 seconds, so 'about a minute' is within range and appropriately approximate.

'Tens of thousands of miles' is the correctly loose version of the commonly cited 60,000-mile estimate — notably, the item did NOT commit to the precise figure, which is the right call given the estimate's softness.

True for the motor pathway the item names: myelinated alpha motor fibres conduct at roughly 70-120 m/s, well above highway speed. The comparison is qualitative and correctly scoped to brain-to-muscle signals rather than all nerves.
Established bone biology — vascularised, innervated, continuously remodelled — stated without any dose, rate or proportion. Corrects a real misconception children hold.
Verified: the auricular muscles are present in everyone and voluntary control is variable. Stated with the correct hedge ('only some people'), no proportion invented.
Verified and non-obvious: the visible lingual papillae are not themselves taste buds; the buds sit in the epithelium along the papillae's walls. A genuine correction of a common misconception.

Retronasal olfaction dominating flavour perception is well established in sensory science, and the blocked-nose observation is the everyday evidence for it. The proportion here ('most of the work') is one of the rare ones in this packet that the literature actually supports.
'About a fifth' matches the standard ~20% of resting metabolic rate for the brain, and the 'even when sitting still' clause is the correct and interesting part.

Verified against NASA: spinal lengthening in microgravity is commonly cited as up to about 3%, roughly two inches for a tall adult, so 'an inch or two' is accurate. The item also actively corrects the 'no gravity in space' misconception with the right explanation (free fall), which is a bonus rather than a defect.

Firmness defect of exactly the type this library has. The first half (fingernails grow faster than toenails) is solidly established; the second half — 'the nails on your dominant hand grow fastest of all' — is stated flatly as fact when the evidence is mixed: it rests largely on Bean's decades-long self-observation, and at least one peer-reviewed comparison found no significant right/left difference. Either drop the dominant-hand clause or mark it as something people have noticed but not settled.
Safe, non-clinical resilience framing that explicitly refuses to tell a reader they shouldn't find hard things hard. No mechanism, dose or proportion claimed.

'the one that changes the most' is an unearned superlative, ranking sleep above every other self-care behaviour with nothing to support the ranking. Sleep's importance is not in doubt; the league table is. Rewrite without the ranking, e.g. 'and one of the ones that changes the most.'
Safe, age-appropriate conflict guidance with no medical or psychological claim beyond common sense. Nothing to overstate.

Defines gratitude honestly and explicitly rules out toxic positivity ('isn't pretending things are fine'), which is the right handling for a young audience. No claim about outcomes or benefits, so nothing to overreach.
